cards.explanation: The complaint is that he fought the Ammonites without calling them. Ephraim, one of Israel's tribes, asks Jephthah, “Why have you crossed over to fight the Ammonites without calling us to go with you?” Picture finding out about the party from the photos afterward. Folks get loud when they feel left out, friends.

The answer is True. Jephthah says, “My people and I had a serious conflict with the Ammonites, and when I called, you did not save me out of their hands.” So in his telling, he called and Ephraim did not save him. Ephraim asks why he went without calling them, and Jephthah says he did call. That's two very different versions of one phone call.

The answer is the LORD. Jephthah says, “…the LORD delivered them into my hand.” He tells Ephraim he risked his life and crossed over, and then he names who gave the win. He doesn't hand the credit to himself. A leader who points up is a good thing to see.

His closing question is, “Why then have you come today to fight against me?” He's just walked through what happened, and then he turns it back on them. I think he's saying, "After all that, this is what you came for?" That's me guessing, friends, but it sure sounds like it.

The answer is False. The text says Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead, fought Ephraim, and “…the men of Gilead struck them down…” Ephraim had come with a threat to burn his house down, and it was Ephraim who was struck down. This part is heavy, friends.

The answer is that the Ephraimites had said, “You Gileadites are fugitives in Ephraim, living in the territories of Ephraim and Manasseh.” That's the insult the text points to. The verse ties those words to the men of Gilead striking Ephraim down.

The answer is Ephraimite. The question at the fords is, “Are you an Ephraimite?” The Gileadites have captured the fords of the Jordan leading to Ephraim. When a fugitive from Ephraim says, “Let me cross over…” that's what they ask him. It's a simple question, and everything hangs on it.

The answer is that he could not pronounce it correctly. The man says “Sibboleth,” “because he could not pronounce it correctly…” and that's how they know him. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the passage, because it ends with men being seized and killed at the fords. It's a hard scene to read, friends.

The answer is False. Jephthah judged Israel six years, and when he died, he was buried “…in one of the cities of Gilead.” That's a city of Gilead, not a burial in Ephraim. The Ephraim burial belongs to Abdon at the end of the passage (Judges 12:15).
